cues.en: You've probably heard of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle from quantum mechanics. That the more you know about a particle's position, the less certain you can be of its momentum and vice versa. Michael here is for you to come away from this video feeling like this is utterly reasonable. It'll take some time, but I think you'll agree that digging deep is well worth it. You see, the uncertainty principle is actually one specific example of a much more general trade-off that shows up in a lot of everyday, totally non-quantum circumstances involving waves.
cues.zh: 你可能听说过量子力学中的海森堡不确定性原理。也就是你对一个粒子的位置了解得越多，对其动量的确定性就越低，反之亦然。我做这个视频的目的，是希望你了解之后能觉得这其实完全合情合理。这需要花点时间，但我相信你会觉得深入探究是完全值得的。你看，不确定性原理其实是一个更通用的权衡特例，这种权衡广泛存在于许多涉及波的日常、完全非量子的场景中。

cues.en: The plan here is to see what this means in the context of sound waves which should feel reasonable and then Doppler radar which should again feel reasonable and a little bit closer to the quantum case and then for particles which if you're willing to accept one or two premises of quantum mechanics hopefully feels just as reasonable as the first two. The core idea here has to do with the interplay between frequency and duration and I bet you already have an intuitive idea of this principle before we even get into the math or the quantum.
cues.zh: 我们接下来的计划是，先看看它在声波中意味着什么——这应该很好理解；然后再看多普勒雷达，这同样合情合理，而且更接近量子的情况；最后再应用到粒子上，如果你愿意接受一两个量子力学的前提，希望它能像前两个例子一样好理解。这里的核心概念与频率和持续时间之间的相互制约有关，我敢打赌，在我们深入数学或量子之前，你其实就已经对这个原理有了直观的感知。

cues.en: If you were to pull up behind a car at a red light and your turn signals were flashing together for a few seconds, you might kind of think that they have the same frequency, but at that point, for all you know, they could fall out of sync as more time passes, revealing that they actually had different frequencies. So an observation over a short period of time gave you low confidence over what their frequencies are. But if you were to set at that red light for a full minute and the signals continued to click in sync,
cues.zh: 如果你在等红灯时停在一辆车后面，你们的转向灯同步闪烁了几秒钟，你可能会觉得它们的频率是一样的；但在那一刻，随着时间推移，它们随时可能会变得不同步，暴露出它们的频率其实并不相同。所以，短时间内的观察只能让你对它们的频率得出较低的把握。但如果你在红灯前停了整整一分钟，转向灯始终保持同步跳动，

cues.en: you would be a lot more confident that the frequencies are actually the same. So that certainty about the frequency information required an observation spread out over time. And this trade-off right here between how short your observation can be and how confident you can feel about the frequency is an example of the general uncertainty principle. Similarly, think of a musical note. The shorter it lasts in time, the less certain you can be about what its exact frequency is.
cues.zh: 你就会更有把握确定它们的频率确实相同。因此，对频率信息的确定性，需要拉长观察时间才能获得。而在观察时间能有多短与对频率有多大把握之间的这种权衡，正是广义不确定性原理的一个典型例子。同样地，想想一个音符：它在时间上持续得越短，你就越难以确定它的确切频率是多少。

cues.en: In the extreme, I could ask you what the pitch of a clap or a shockwave is, and even someone with perfect pitch would be unable to answer. And on the flip side, a more definite frequency requires a longer duration signal. Or rather than talking about definiteness or certainty, it would be a little more accurate here to say that the short signal correlates highly with a wider range of frequency, and that the signal correlating strongly with only a narrow range of frequencies must last for a longer time.
cues.zh: 在极端情况下，如果我问你拍手声或冲击波的音高是多少，即便是拥有绝对音感的人也无法回答。反过来说，想要得到更确定的频率，就需要更长持续时间的信号。或者与其谈论确定性，这里更准确的说法是：短信号与较宽的频率范围高度相关，而只与极窄频率范围强相关的信号，必然需要持续更长的时间。

cues.en: Here, that's the kind of phrase that's made a little bit clearer when we bring in the actual math. So let's turn now to talking about the 48 transform, which is the relevant construct for analyzing frequencies. The last video I put out was a visual intuition for this transform, and yes, it probably would be helpful if you've seen it, but I'm gonna go ahead and give a quick recap here just to remind ourselves of how it went. Let's say you have a signal and it plays five beats per second over the course of two seconds.
cues.zh: 结合真正的数学原理，这种说法会更好理解一些。那么现在我们来聊聊傅里叶变换，它是分析频率的关键工具。我上一期视频讲了这种变换的直观视觉理解，看过当然会有所帮助，不过我还是先带大家快速回顾一下。假设有一个信号，在两秒的时间内每秒振动 5 次。

cues.en: The Fourier transform gives a way to view any signal not in terms of the intensity at each point in time, but instead in terms of the strength of various frequencies within it. The main idea was to take this signal and to kind of wind it around a circle. As in, imagine some rotating vector whose length is determined by the height of the graph at each point in time. Right now, this little vector is rotating at 0.3 cycles per second. That's the frequency with which we're winding the graph around the circle.
cues.zh: 傅里叶变换提供了一种全新的视角：不再观察信号在各时间点的强度，而是看其中各个频率分量的强弱。核心思路是把这个信号“缠绕”在一个圆上。也就是说，想象一个旋转向量，它的长度由图表在每个时刻的高度决定。此时，这个小向量正以每秒 0.3 圈的速度旋转。这就是我们将图表缠绕在圆上的频率。

cues.en: And for most frequencies, the signal is kind of just averaged out over the circle. This was the fun part of last video, don't you think? Just seeing the different patterns that come up as you wind a pure cosine around a circle like this. But the key point is what happens when that winding frequency matches the signal frequency, in this case five cycles per second. As our little vector is rotating around and it draws, all of the peaks line up on one side and all of the valleys on another side.
cues.zh: 对大多数频率来说，信号在圆周上基本都被相互抵消扯平了。这也是上一期视频最有趣的地方，看着把一个纯余弦波像这样绕在圆上时呈现出的各种奇妙图案。但关键在于：当缠绕频率与信号本身的频率一致时——比如这里的每秒 5 圈——会发生什么。随着小向量边旋转边绘制，所有的波峰都排在一侧，而所有的波谷都集中在另一侧。

cues.en: So the whole weight of the graph is kind of off-center, so to speak. The idea behind the Fourier transform is that if you follow the center of mass of the wound-up graph with frequency f, the position of that center of mass encodes the strength of that frequency in the original signal. The distance between that center of mass and the origin captures the strength of that frequency. And this is something I didn't really talk about in the main video, but the angle of that center of mass off the horizontal
cues.zh: 因此可以说，整个图表的重心就偏离了中心。傅里叶变换的核心思想就在于，如果去追踪以频率 f 缠绕后的图形质心，这个质心的位置就编码了原信号中该频率的强度。质心到原点的距离，反映的就是该频率的强弱。另外我在主视频里没细讲的是，质心与水平轴的夹角

cues.en: corresponds to the phase of the given frequency. Now one way to think of this whole winding mechanism is that it's a way to measure how well your signal correlates with a given pure frequency. So remember when we say the Fourier transform we're referring to this new function whose input is that winding frequency and whose output is the center of mass thought of as a complex number. Or more technically it's a certain multiple of that center of mass but whatever the overall shape remains the same.
cues.zh: 对应的正是该频率的相位。我们可以把整套缠绕机制理解为一种度量方式，用来衡量你的信号与某个给定纯频率的相关程度。请记住，当我们说“傅里叶变换”时，指的就是这样一个新函数：输入是缠绕频率，输出是被视为复数的质心位置。更严格地讲，它是质心的某个倍数，但无论如何整体形态是一样的。

cues.en: And the graph that I'm drawing is just going to be the x-coordinate of that center of mass, the real part of its output. If you wanted, you could also plot the distance between the center of mass and the origin, and maybe that better conveys how strongly each possible frequency correlates with the signal. The downside is that you lose some of the nice linearity properties that I talked about last video. Anyway, point is, this spike you're looking at here, above the winding frequency of 5, is the Fourier transform's way of telling us that the dominant frequency of the signal is 5 beats per second.
cues.zh: 我画的这张图，其实就是那个质心的 x 坐标，也就是输出的实部。如果你愿意，也可以画质心到原点的距离，那也许更能说明每个可能频率与信号的相关程度有多强。缺点是，你会失去我上个视频讲到的一些漂亮的线性性质。总之，重点是，你在这里看到的、位于缠绕频率 5 上方的这个尖峰，就是傅里叶变换在告诉我们：信号的主导频率是每秒 5 拍。

cues.en: And equally importantly, the fact that it's a little bit spread out around that 5 is an indication that pure sine waves near 5 beats per second also correlate pretty well with the signal. And that last idea is key for the uncertainty principle. What I want you to do is think about how this spread changes as the signal persists longer or shorter over time. You've already seen this at an intuitive level. All we're doing right now is just illustrating it in the language of Fourier transforms.
cues.zh: 同样重要的是，它在 5 附近稍微散开，这说明接近每秒 5 拍的纯正弦波也与该信号相关性很好。而最后这个想法正是理解不确定性原理的关键。我想让你思考的是：当信号在时间上持续得更久或更短时，这种展宽会怎样变化。你已经在直觉层面见过这一点。我们现在做的，只是用傅里叶变换的语言把它说明白。

cues.en: If the signal persists over a long period of time, then when the winding frequency is even slightly different from 5, the signal goes on long enough to wrap itself around the circle and balance out. So looking at the Fourier plot over here, that corresponds to a super sharp drop-off in the magnitude of the transform as your frequency shifts away from that 5 beats per second. On the other hand, if your signal was really localized to a short period of time,
cues.zh: 如果信号持续很长时间，那么当缠绕频率哪怕稍微偏离 5 时，信号也会持续足够久，在圆上绕圈并相互抵消。所以看这边的傅里叶图，这对应的是：当频率偏离每秒 5 拍时，变换的幅度会极其陡峭地下降。另一方面，如果你的信号真的只局限在很短的一段时间内，

cues.en: Then as you adjust the frequency away from 5 beats per second, the signal doesn't really have as much time to balance itself out around the circle. You have to change the winding frequency to be meaningfully different from 5 before that signal starts to balance out again. Over on the frequency plot, that corresponds to a much broader peak around the 5 beats per second. And that's the uncertainty principle, just phrased a little bit more mathematically. A signal concentrated in time must have a spread-out Fourier transform,
cues.zh: 那么当你把频率调离每秒 5 拍时，信号并没有那么多时间在圆上自我抵消。你得把缠绕频率改成与 5 有明显差异，信号才会重新开始抵消。在频率图上，这对应的是每秒 5 拍附近一个宽得多的峰。这就是不确定性原理，只是换成了稍微更数学化的说法。一个在时间上集中的信号，其傅里叶变换必然是展宽的，

cues.en: meaning it correlates with a wide range of frequencies and a signal with a concentrated Fourier transform has to be spread out in time. And one other place where this comes up in a really tangible way is Doppler radar. So with radar the idea is you send out some radio wave pulse and the pulse might reflect off of objects and the time that it takes for this echo signal to return to you lets you deduce how far away those objects are.
cues.zh: 意思是它与很宽范围的频率相关；而一个傅里叶变换集中的信号，在时间上就必须是展宽的。另一个能非常具体地体现这一点的地方是多普勒雷达。雷达的原理是：你发出某个无线电波脉冲，脉冲可能从物体上反射，而回波信号返回所需的时间，让你能推断那些物体有多远。

cues.en: And you can actually take this one step further and make deductions about the velocities of those objects using the Doppler effect. Think about sending out a pulse with some frequency. If this gets reflected off an object moving towards you, then the beats of that wave get kind of smooshed together, so the echo you hear back is going to be a slightly higher frequency. Fourier transforms give a neat way to view this. The Fourier transform of your original signal tells you the frequencies that go into it,
cues.zh: 实际上，你还可以更进一步，利用多普勒效应来推断这些物体的速度。想象一下发射一个带有特定频率的脉冲。如果它被一个朝你移动的物体反射，波的节拍就会被压缩在一起，接收到的回波频率就会略高一些。傅里叶变换提供了一个非常巧妙的视角来观察这一点。原始信号的傅里叶变换展示了它包含的各种频率成分，

cues.en: And for simplicity, let's think of that as being dominated by a single pure frequency. Though, as you know, if it's a short pulse, that means that our Fourier transform has to be spread out a little bit. And now think about the Doppler shift at echo. By coming back at a higher frequency, it means that the Fourier transform will just look like a similar plot shifted up a bit. Moreover, if you look at the size of that shift, you can deduce how quickly the object was moving. By the way, there is an important technical point that I'm choosing to gloss over here.
cues.zh: 为简单起见，我们先假设它主要由单一的纯频率构成。不过正如你所知，如果是一个短脉冲，傅里叶变换就必然会有所展宽。现在再来看看产生多普勒频移的回波。频率变高意味着其傅里叶变换就像是原有图像向上平移了一点。此外，通过观察这个偏移量的大小，就能推算出物体的运动速度。顺便提一句，这里我略过了一个重要的技术细节，

cues.en: And I've outlined it a little more in the video description. What follows is meant to be a distilled, if somewhat oversimplified description of the Fourier tradeoff in this setup. The salient fact is that time and frequency of that echo signal correspond respectively to the position and the velocity of the object being measured. Which is what makes this example much more closely analogous to the quantum mechanical Heisenberg uncertainty principle. You see, there is a very real way in which a radar operator faces a dilemma.
cues.zh: 我在视频简介里对此做了更详细的说明。接下来要讲的，是对这种场景下傅里叶权衡关系的一种提炼，虽然略有简化。关键事实在于，回波信号的时间和频率分别对应被测物体的位置和速度。这正是该例子能极好地类比量子力学中海森堡不确定性原理的原因。你看，雷达操作员确确实实面临着一个两难境地：

cues.en: where the more certain you can be about the positions of things, the less certain you are about their velocities. Here, imagine sending out a pulse that persists over a long period of time. Then that means the echo from some object is also spread out over time. And on its own, that might not seem like an issue. But in practice, there's all sorts of different objects in the field, so these echoes are all going to start to get overlapped with each other. Combine that with other noise and imperfections,
cues.zh: 你对物体的位置越确定，对其速度就越不确定。试想一下，如果发射一个持续时间很长的脉冲，就意味着从物体反射回来的回波在时间上也是展宽的。单看这一个脉冲可能不算问题，但在实际环境中会有各种各样的物体，这些回波就会开始相互重叠。再加上环境噪声和其他干扰，

cues.en: and this can make the locations of multiple objects extremely ambiguous. Instead, a more precise understanding of how far away all these things are would require having a very quick little pulse confined to a small amount of time. But think about the frequency representations of such a short echo. As you saw with the sound example, the Fourier transform of a quick pulse is necessarily more spread out. So for many objects with various velocities, that would mean that the Doppler shifted echoes
cues.zh: 这会让多个物体的位置变得极其模糊。相反，如果想更精确地掌握物体的距离，就需要一个时间极短的短脉冲。但考虑一下这种短回波在频域上的表现：正如刚才声音示例所展示的，短脉冲的傅里叶变换必然更分散。因此对于以不同速度运动的多个物体，产生多普勒频移的回波

cues.en: despite having been nicely separated in time, are more likely to overlap in frequency space. So since what you're looking at is the sum of all of these, it can be really ambiguous how you break it down. If you wanted a nice clean sharp view of the velocities, you would need to have an echo that only occupies a very small amount of frequency space. But for a signal to be concentrated in frequency space, it necessarily has to be spread out in time.
cues.zh: 尽管在时间上被很好地分开了，但在频域中却更有可能相互重叠。由于你看到的是所有回波的叠加，想要将其分解开来就会极其困难。如果你想清晰利落地测量出速度，回波就必须在频域上只占据极小的范围；但一个信号要想在频域高度集中，就必然会在时域上大幅展宽。

cues.en: This is the Fourier trade-off. You cannot have crisp delineation for both. And this brings us to the quantum case. Do you know who else spent some time immersed in the pragmatic world of radio wave transmissions? A young, otherwise philosophically inclined history major in World War I France, Louis de Broglie. And this was a strangely fitting post, given his predispositions to philosophizing about the nature of waves. Because after the war, as de Broglie switched from the humanities to physics, in his 1924 PhD thesis,
cues.zh: 这就是傅里叶权衡。你无法让两者都拥有清晰的界限。这就引出了量子的情况。你知道还有谁曾在无线电波传输的实用世界里钻研过吗？一战时期法国的一位年轻历史专业学生，平时热衷于哲学思考，名叫 Louis de Broglie。鉴于他热衷于对波的本质进行哲学思考，这个岗位出奇地适合他。因为战后，de Broglie 从人文学科转向了物理学，在他 1924 年的博士论文中，

cues.en: he proposed that all matter has wave-like properties. And more than that, he concluded that the momentum of any moving particle is going to be proportional to the spatial frequency of that wave. How many times that wave cycles per unit distance. Okay, now that's the kind of phrase that can easily fly into one ear and out the other. Because as soon as you say matter is a wave, it's easy to just throw up your hands and say physics is just weird. But really, think about this.
cues.zh: 他提出所有物质都具有波动性。不仅如此，他还得出结论：任何运动粒子的动量，都正比于该波的空间频率。也就是该波在单位距离内循环振动的次数。好了，这种话很容易左耳进右耳出。因为一旦说物质是一种波，大家很容易两手一摊，觉得物理学就是这么匪夷所思。但认真想想看。

cues.en: Even if you're willing to grant that particles behave like waves in some way, whatever that means, why on earth should the momentum of those particles, the thing we classically think of as mass times velocity, have anything to do with the spatial frequency of that wave? Now, being more of a math than a physics guy, I asked a number of people with deeper backgrounds in physics about helpful intuitions here, and one thing that became clear is that there is a surprising variety of viewpoints.
cues.zh: 即使你愿意承认粒子在某种程度上表现得像波（无论这代表什么），那粒子的动量——也就是我们在经典力学里理解的质量乘以速度——到底凭什么会和该波的空间频率扯上关系？作为一个偏数学而非物理出身的人，我就此请教了许多有深厚物理背景的人，希望能获得一些直观的理解，而有一点非常明确，那就是大家的视角多得惊人。

cues.en: Now, personally, one thing I found to be interesting was just going back to the source and seeing how De Broglie framed things in his seminal paper on the topic. You see, there is a sense in which it's not all that different from the Doppler Effect, where relative movement corresponds to shifts in frequency. It has a slightly different flavor, since we're not talking about frequency over time, instead we're talking about frequency over space, and special relativity is going to come into play, but I still think it's an interesting analogy.
cues.zh: 就我个人而言，我觉得很有意思的一件事是直接回到源头，看看 De Broglie 在他开创性的论文中是如何构想这件事的。你看，在某种意义上，这和多普勒效应并没有太大区别，在多普勒效应中，相对运动对应着频率的改变。两者的感觉稍有不同，因为我们谈论的不是时间上的频率，而是空间上的频率，而且狭义相对论也会介入其中，但我依然认为这是个很有启发性的类比。

cues.en: In his thesis, de Broglie lays out what is, in his own words, a crude comparison for the kind of wave phenomenon he has in mind. Imagine many weights hanging from springs, with all of these weights oscillating up and down in sync, and with most of the mass concentrated towards a single point. The energy of these oscillating weights is meant to be a metaphor for the energy of a particle, specifically the E equals mc squared-style energy residing in its mass.
cues.zh: 在他的论文中，de Broglie 用他自己的话阐述了一个粗略的类比，来说明他所构想的波动现象。想象许多悬挂在弹簧上的重物，所有这些重物都同步上下振动，并且大部分质量集中在某一个点附近。这些振动重物的能量，是用来比喻粒子的能量，具体来说就是蕴含在其质量中的“E 等于 mc 平方”式的能量。

cues.en: And de Broglie emphasized how the conception he had in mind involves the particle being dispersed across all of space. The whole premise he was exploring here is that the energy of a particle might have to do with something that oscillates over time, since this was known to be the case for photons. And these oscillating weights are just meant to be a metaphor for whatever that something might be. With Einstein's relatively new theory of relativity in mind, he pointed out that if you view this whole setup while moving relative to it,
cues.zh: de Broglie 强调，他的构想涉及粒子分散在整个空间中。他在此探索的整个前提是：粒子的能量可能与某种随时间振动的东西有关，因为人们已知光子就是这种情况。而这些振动的重物，只是用来比喻那具体可能是什么东西而已。结合 Einstein 当时还算新鲜的相对论，他指出，如果你在与整个装置发生相对运动时去观察它，

cues.en: all of the weights are going to appear to fall out of phase. That's not obvious, and I'm certainly exaggerating the effect in this animation. It has to do with a core fact from special relativity that what you consider to be simultaneous events in one reference frame may not be simultaneous in a different reference frame. So even though from one point of view, you might see two of these weights as reaching their peaks and their valleys at the same instant, from a different moving point of view, those events might actually be happening at different times.
cues.zh: 所有的重物看起来就会出现相位不同步。这并不直观，而且我在这段动画里显然夸大了这种效果。这与狭义相对论的一个核心事实有关：你在一个参考系中认为是同时发生的事件，在另一个参考系中可能并不是同时的。因此，尽管从某一个视角来看，你可能会看到其中两个重物在同一瞬间到达波峰和波谷，但从另一个处于运动中的视角来看，这些事件实际发生的时间可能并不相同。

cues.en: Understanding this more fully requires some knowledge of special relativity, so we'll all just have to wait for Henry Reich's series on that topic to come out. Right here, our only goal is to get an inkling for why momentum, that thing we usually think of as mass times velocity, should have anything to do with spatial frequency. And the basic line of reasoning here is if mass is the same as energy via E equals mc squared, and if that energy was carried as some kind of oscillating phenomenon, similar to how it is for photons,
cues.zh: 要更完整地理解这一点，需要一些狭义相对论知识，所以我们只能等 Henry Reich 关于这个主题的系列视频出来。眼下，我们唯一的目标是初步理解：为什么动量——我们通常理解成质量乘以速度的那个东西——会和空间频率扯上关系。基本推理是这样的：如果通过 E=mc²，质量等同于能量，而那种能量又是以某种振荡现象的形式携带的，类似于光子的情况，

cues.en: then this sort of relativistic Doppler effect means changes to how that mass moves corresponds to changes in the spatial frequency. So what does our general Fourier trade-off tell us in this case? Well, if a particle is described as a little wave packet over space, then the Fourier transform, where we're thinking of this as a function over space, not over time, tells us how much various pure frequencies correspond with this top wave.
cues.zh: 那么这种相对论多普勒效应就意味着，质量运动方式的改变对应于空间频率的改变。那么在这种情况下，我们一般的傅里叶权衡告诉我们什么？如果粒子被描述为空间中的一个小波包，那么傅里叶变换——这里我们把它看作空间上的函数，而不是时间上的函数——会告诉我们各个纯频率与这个波包有多大的对应关系。

cues.en: So if the momentum is the spatial frequency up to a constant multiple, then the momentum is also a kind of wave, namely some multiple of the Fourier transform of the original wave. So if that original wave was very concentrated around a single point, as we have seen multiple times now, that means that its Fourier transform must necessarily be more spread out, and hence the wave describing its momentum must be more spread out, and vice versa. Notice.
cues.zh: 所以，如果动量在相差一个常数倍的意义上就是空间频率，那么动量也是一种波，也就是原波的傅里叶变换的某个倍数。所以，如果原波非常集中在单点附近——我们现在已经多次看到这种情况——那就意味着它的傅里叶变换必然更加分散，因此描述其动量的波也必然更加分散，反之亦然。注意。

cues.en: Unlike the Doppler radar case where the ambiguity arose because waves were being used to measure an object with a definite distance and speed, what we're saying here is that the particle is the wave. So the spread out over space and over momentum is not some artifact of imperfect measurement techniques. It's a spread fundamental to what the particle is, analogous to how a musical note being spread out over time is fundamental to what it even means to be a musical note.
cues.zh: 与多普勒雷达的情况不同——那里出现模糊是因为用波去测量一个具有确定距离和速度的物体——我们这里说的是，粒子本身就是波。因此，在空间上和动量上的分散，并不是不完美测量技术造成的某种假象。这种分散是粒子本质所固有的，类似于一个音符在时间上展开，是它之所以成为音符的根本所在。

cues.en: One pet peeve I have in mainstream references to quantum is that they often treat Heisenberg's uncertainty principle as some fundamental example of things being unknowable in the quantum realm, as if it is a core nugget of the universe's indeterminacy. But really it's just a trade-off between how concentrated a wave and its frequency representation can be, applied to the premise that matter is some kind of wave and hence spread out. All of the stuff about randomness and unknowability is still there, but it comes one level deeper.
cues.zh: 我对主流量子科普有一个不满：它们常把海森堡不确定性原理当成量子领域中事物不可知的根本范例，好像它是宇宙不确定性的核心。但实际上，它只是关于一个波及其频率表示能有多集中的权衡，并被应用到“物质是某种波、因而会分散”这一前提上。所有关于随机性和不可知性的内容仍然存在，只是深入了一层。

cues.en: in the way that these waves have come to be interpreted. You see, when you measure these particles, say trying to detect if it's in a given region, whether or not you find it there appears to be probabilistic, where the probability of finding it is proportional to the strength of the wave in that region. So when one of these waves is concentrated near a point, what that actually means is that we have a higher probability of finding it near that point, that we are more certain of its location.
cues.zh: 就体现在这些波如今被解释的方式上。你看，当你测量这些粒子时，比如说试图探测它是否在某个给定区域，你能否在那里找到它似乎是概率性的，找到它的概率正比于波在该区域的强度。所以，当这些波中的某一个集中在某点附近时，这实际意味着我们在该点附近找到它的概率更高，也就是我们更确定它的位置。

cues.en: And just to beat this drum one more time, since that concentration implies a more spread-out Fourier transform, then the wave describing its momentum would also be more spread out, so you wouldn't be able to find a narrow range of momenta that the particle has a high probability of occupying. I quite like how if you look at the German word for this principle, it might be more directly translated as the unsharpness relation, which I think more faithfully captures the Fourier trade-off at play here without imposing on questions of no ability.
cues.zh: 再强调一次：既然空间上的集中意味着傅里叶变换会更加分散，那么描述其动量的波也会更加发散，你也就无法找到一个粒子有极大概率处于其中的狭窄动量范围。我很喜欢这个原理对应的德语词，它更直白的翻译大概是“不清晰关系”，我认为这更准确地体现了这里起作用的傅里叶权衡，而没有牵扯到可知性相关的哲学问题。

cues.en: When I think of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, what makes it fascinating is not so much that it's a statement about randomness. I mean, yes, that randomness is very thought-provoking and contentious and just plain weird. But to me, equally fascinating is that underpinning Heisenberg's conclusion is that position and momentum have the same relationship as sound and frequency, as if a particle's momentum is somehow the sheet music describing how it moves through space.
cues.zh: 每当我想起海森堡不确定性原理，觉得最迷人的其实并不在于它阐释了随机性。我是说，没错，那种随机性确实发人深省、充满争议，而且极其诡异。但在我看来，同样迷人的是支撑海森堡结论的底层逻辑：位置与动量的关系，其实就如同声音与频率的关系一样，仿佛粒子的动量就是谱写它在空间中如何运动的一纸乐谱。
